item.title: The Performance Cost of Node.js and GraphQL
A Hyper-Dense City
item.description:
Score 3 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @emberfiend
October 8, 2023 | https://judybackhouse.com/fiction/ultra-high-density-city.html | archive.org

I read about extinct animals and wildfires, about dwindling rainforests and heat waves, and I conclude that we have made too much of an impact. It's good to be a successful apex predator, but not at the expense of the planet and all the other species that could live here.

So, I was wondering, how can we make less of an impact? Yes, we can recycle our plastic containers, buy second-hand clothes, take the bus instead of a car. We can vote for responsible politicians and hold them to account. We can invent carbon credits and try to motivate businesses to change their ways, but none of it seems to be enough. I think we need to do more. Doing more starts with using less, and I mean a lot less, radically less.

So, I conducted a thought experiment. How small could we make our cities? I don't just mean 'tiny homes' ingeniously fitted with every mod con, including space for a shoe collection. I was trying to work out what is the minimum space I would be prepared to live in? What kind of space and society would have the least planetary impact while still enabling an interesting life?

I am a nerdy introvert who likes my own company, so I would want a private space; some closed volume that is mine alone, where I can escape to. It doesn't have to be big. I am writing this in a room which measures 2 x 3 x 2,5 meters or 15 cubic meters. That is big enough for a divan, two tables and two bookshelves. I don't sleep in this space, but I'd be happy to. When I first saw this room, I thought it was too small to be called a bedroom, but I've adapted my expectations and I now feel very comfortable here. So, my starting point was to design a city in which each person has 15 cubic meters of personal, private space.

What would make it feasible and comfortable to live in such a small space? Well, there would be no kitchen or living room or dining room, as we expect in our homes, but we could overcome these deprivations with changes to how we live. How many other activities of living can move outside of the private space? Food preparation and eating could happen in communal kitchens. Work already happens in co-work spaces. Shared laundry services already exist. We could entertain at restaurants or in parks. Entertainment is provided on small private screens or at public events. We could swim in public swimming pools, work out in public gyms, garden in public gardens. If we can move all activities other than sleeping, dressing and musing out of private space, we can radically reduce the amount of space we need to live well. (I admit I got stuck on shared bathrooms. No doubt my middle-class fastidiousness. I have shared bathrooms at campsites, so it is not impossible.)

One very desirable consequence would be owning a lot less. I would not need a kitchen or all the things that are used for food preparation. I would not need a washing machine, garden tools, living room furniture. If equipment for creative pursuits and cloud storage were ubiquitous, we could dispense with most of our private belongings. Imagine if we each owned nothing more than a few changes of clothing, perhaps a few treasured artefacts and some personal tools, like a computing device, a musical instrument, or some favourite paintbrushes. To live like this, with radically less, but still enjoying rich, enjoyable and creative lives, we'd need a city full of accessible shared services. Services are accessible if they exist nearby and are free to use.

This led me to think about a hyper-dense city where all these services are available in one space. Could we access everything on foot? No cars, no busses, no metros, no roads, no parking garages. Imagine how that would reduce the space needed. This gave me the idea of a city in which everything is within one kilometre. One thousand meters is easy for most healthy humans to walk. (And we could provide exoskeletons, for those with mobility issues.)

Just how dense could a city be? Here is the state of my thought experiment.

Imagine a cylinder, about as tall as it is wide. This cylinder is the entire city. Not a city of buildings, but a single building that is a city. If our cylinder is 1 kilometre high, with a diameter of 1 kilometre, it will contain a volume of 785 398 163 cubic meters. Let's try to fit a city into that.

Assuming some people will want to look out from their tiny private rooms, these could be around the edge of the city. Imagine a 'skin', some 20 meters thick, that surrounds the city from the first floor (one above ground) to the top. This skin has a volume of 74 141 587 cubic meters. If each person needs a 15 cubic meter interior and allowing 10% more for structural elements, we can accommodate 4 493 429 people in this skin. Somewhere between 4 and 5 million people sounds like a good size for a city of the future.

Clever folding of the exterior may provide more privacy and sunlight and we would want built-in platforms to support plants, because a plant-covered city will be cooler and more attractive. The sleep spaces would open onto walkways, protected with screens, that edge the inner side of the cylinder. The walkways would provide access to elevators, stairs between levels, as well as walkways out into the central volume. That central volume, all 1 056 831 769 cubic meters of it, would contain the shared public spaces and city services. So, what would that look like?

Our city will not need much retail or manufacturing space. Without as much stuff being produced, sold and transported, most people will work less and have more leisure. So, we will need a lot more space for eating and socialising. Bars, cafes, restaurants and canteens must abound. Also parks, sports facilities, libraries, reading rooms, clubs and, of course, holodecks. There will, of course, be offices, workshops, lecture rooms, laboratories, studios, and fabrication spaces.

The city will provide these spaces on platforms; some small enough to be a cosy café, some large enough to be a football stadium, and many sizes in between. All the platforms (and walkways) would have substantial walls, transparent or opaque, to remove any fear of falling. Some would be closed with a roof, while others might be open above (if we can figure out how to build an overall transparent roof at the top of the city).

Most platforms will be stacked, for structural purposes, but also to maximise natural light penetration. I imagine they would look like giant, snaking tree-trunks, some round in cross-section, others square or hexagonal, rising sinuously up the central volume of the city. Some platforms might float alone, or in small clusters. The platforms would connect with walkways, elevators and escalators, some wide and some narrow, forming the lanes, byways, footpaths and roads of the city. I imagine that the inside volume of the city will look like a giant, dense forest strung with vines.

We could, of course, excavate down too, providing additional levels to accommodate waste processing, water purification, power generation and server farms; all the background stuff that can operate in enclosed spaces. I've got some ideas about agriculture too which I'll address in another post.

I would surround my city with a giant park; a 10-kilometer-wide strip of lawns and gardens, rivers and lakes, with recreation facilities. Access to the park would be from any part of the ground floor of the building. I imagine that this level will be open on all sides, with concentric rows of pillars to hold up the outer wall of the city above. There would be one high-speed railway line running through this park to connect the city to neighbouring cities. With everything provided in the city, travel will be the exception rather than the norm. I plan to rewild all the land outside of the city. Since my reference city is Johannesburg (in South Africa) that would mean a very substantial game fence surrounding the whole.

It doesn't take long to realise that this kind of hyper-dense city would require not only changes to the physical space but also extensive social re-engineering. For example, we are doing away with family living units, and providing space only for individuals. How does that work? I have written a short story, set in this hyper-dense city, to explore the social consequences. I plan to write more. If you are interested, sign up to my newsletter to hear when those get published.

Many modern housing solutions which try to increase density, provide low-cost housing, reduce the use of cars, and to reconfigure personal space are interesting, but do not go far enough. Mostly, they only affect a few. We need to change the way vast numbers of people live. We can provide everyone with a decent living space, and reduce our planetary impact, if we all have small private spaces and share the things we need for a comfortable life. This is my 'far enough'; my extreme vision of how we can make a just world, putting an end to overconsumption and radically changing our society for a different future.

What do you think? Could humans reinvent their cities and their lifestyles like this?

item.title: Flexoki
item.description:
Score 3 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @simonpure
October 8, 2023 | https://stephango.com/flexoki | archive.org

Flexoki is an inky color scheme for prose and code. Flexoki is designed for reading and writing on digital screens. It is inspired by analog printing inks and warm shades of paper.

Flexoki is minimalistic and high-contrast. The colors are calibrated for legibility and perceptual balance across devices and when switching between light and dark modes.

Flexoki is open-source under the MIT license. Flexoki is available for many popular apps listed below, including Obsidian using my theme Minimal.

Color palette

Flexoki is the color palette used on this site. To switch between light and dark mode press the D key or use the toggle at the top of the page. Click the swatches to copy a color to your clipboard.

Syntax highlighting

You can find examples of code on the pages for Tidy Reader and Tidy URL.

Base tones

Flexoki uses warm monochromatic base tones that blend the black ink tone with the base paper tone. 8 colors are used in light and dark mode:

  • 3 text colors: normal, muted, faint
  • 3 interface colors: normal, hover, active
  • 2 background colors: primary, secondary

Incremental values can be derived using opacity. For example, you can use a 60% opacity black tone on top of the paper tone to create the 600 value.

Hex Color Light theme Dark theme
#100F0F black tx bg
#1C1B1A 950   bg-2
#282726 900   ui
#343331 850   ui-2
#403E3C 800   ui-3
#575653 700   tx-3
#6F6E69 600 tx-2  
#878580 500   tx-2
#B7B5AC 300 tx-3  
#CECDC3 200 ui-3 tx
#DAD8CE 150 ui-2  
#E6E4D9 100 ui  
#F2F0E5 50 bg-2  
#FFFCF0 paper bg  

Colors

8 colors are available for accents and syntax highlighting. Each color is available in two tones calibrated for light and dark modes.

In the future, a full range of tones from 50 to 950 will be added. Unlike the base tones, colors cannot be blended using opacity because this desaturates the pigment effect. More on this topic below.

Dark tones

Hex Color Light theme Dark theme
#AF3029 red re re-2
#BC5215 orange or or-2
#AD8301 yellow ye ye-2
#66800B green gr gr-2
#24837B cyan cy cy-2
#205EA6 blue bl bl-2
#5E409D purple pu pu-2
#A02F6F magenta ma ma-2

Light tones

Hex Color Light theme Dark theme
#D14D41 red re-2 re
#DA702C orange or-2 or
#D0A215 yellow ye-2 ye
#879A39 green gr-2 gr
#3AA99F cyan cy-2 cy
#4385BE blue bl-2 bl
#8B7EC8 purple pu-2 pu
#CE5D97 magenta ma-2 ma

Why?

I created Flexoki for my personal site, stephango.com. You’re reading it now. I wanted the colors to feel distinctive yet familiar. Like ink on paper.

The name Flexoki comes from flexography — a common printing process for paper and cardboard1. I spent many years working with dyes and inks particularly for my companies Inkodye and Lumi. I also have a fascination with digital paper. I wanted to bring the comfort of analog color to emissive digital screens.

One challenge is that ink on paper is a subtractive process whereas LCD and OLED screens use additive color. Replicating the effect of mixing pigments digitally is difficult. The following video illustrates the problem:

See the full SIGGRAPH 2021 talk

Mixing blue and yellow paint creates green, whereas digital color mixing results in a brownish hue. Watercolors retain their saturation when you dilute them, whereas reducing the opacity of digital colors makes them look desaturated.

Another challenge with digital color is human perception across color spaces. For example, yellow appears much brighter than blue. Ethan Schoonover’s color scheme Solarized (2011) was an important inspiration for Flexoki. His emphasis on CIELAB lightness relationships helped me understand how to find colors that appear cohesive.

I found that choosing colors with perfect perceptual consistency can be at odds with the distinctiveness of colors in practical applications like syntax highlighting. If you adhere too closely to evenness in perceptual lightness you can end up with a palette that looks washed out and difficult to parse.

Solving for all these problems is how I arrived at Flexoki. I wish it could have been more science than art, but it wasn’t. Some day I hope to arrive at a more reliable way to generate digital color palettes that respect the constraints I laid out. In the meantime, I hope you find this iteration of Flexoki useful.

Ports

Flexoki is available for the following apps and tools.

Apps

  • Alacritty
  • Emacs
  • iTerm2
  • Kitty
  • macOS Terminal
  • Neovim
  • Obsidian and included with Minimal
  • Sublime Text
  • VS Code
  • Warp
  • WezTerm
  • Windows Terminal
  • Xresources

Frameworks

  • Shadcn
  • Tailwind
  • theme.sh

Other

  • Figma
  • GIMP

Contributing

Flexoki is MIT licensed. You are free to port Flexoki to any app. Please include attribution and a link to stephango.com/flexoki. You can submit your port to the list via pull request on the Flexoki repo.

Changelog

Date  
2023-10-07 Initial release

item.title: Design Principles to Build With
item.description:
Score 9 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @Tomte
October 8, 2023 | https://pketh.org/design-principles.html | archive.org

This post is adapted from a talk I did at the Design Matters conference in Copenhagen.

I’ve been working on Kinopio for over 4 years now. It’s felt more like building a house, piling up little bricks and wood planks, just a little bit each day. Except that, this house is never finished.

Something I learned from my time at Glitch, was that before you get too deep into the process of building, you should write out a short list of product design principles.

The more unique and definitive your values are, the more useful they’ll be as a decision making tool later on.

These are some of the principles that I use to design (and redesign) Kinopio:

1. Embrace smallness
2. Build for fidget-ability
3. Embrace plain text
4. A single interface for mobile and desktop
5. Refine by pruning

Principle #1

Embrace Smallness by Embracing Code as a Living Design System

Being bootstrapped means that resources are tight. But that’s it’s own kind of blessing. When you feel constrained, you’re naturally drawn to simple and basic tools and processes.

When planning out a new feature, instead of using design software to draw and arrange buttons, inputs, and dialog windows into detailed mockups, I skip all that and jump right into real code with <button>, <input>, and <dialog> elements.

Here’s the HTML part of a dialog window component (using pug):

<template lang="pug">
dialog.narrow.dialog-name(v-if="visible" :open="visible")
  section
    p blank dialog, please duplicate
  section
    button(@click="incrementBy")
      span Count is: 
    p Current theme is: 
</template>

Which produces:

In the spirit of keeping things simple, the UI is described mostly using regular HTML tags and the layout basically designs itself.

The way that works architecturally, is there’s a global parent file (App.vue in my case because I use vue.js) which contains global styles that all the other child components inherit from.

Relatedly, it’s pretty satisfying to make things that are efficient, small, and fast. Maybe it’s the craft-like part of engineering.

Embracing smallness also means being diligent about only adding small third-party dependencies and utility libs that do one simple thing like date manipulation or generating random colors.

Partly because of this, Kinopio only weighs ~220kb with libs and assets. So in an alternate dimension where we didn’t have the Internet, but still had HTML, I’d ship kinopio to you on a single 3.5mm floppy disk (and it wouldn’t even need to be a high-density one)

Principle #2

Building for Fidget-Ability, hmmm

The first time I really thought about fidgeting was in the early 2000s when I learned that the faceted curves on this Japanese cell phone were explicitly designed for you to run your fingers over when you weren’t using it.

Software Design is usually focused on capturing user inputs and showing outputs. But most of the time we spend using software tools, we’re actually in between those two actively engaged states.

This is what I call the “hmmm” state.

As in, “hmmm, what should I write next?” Or, “hmmm, I’m highlighting this text while reading it to help me focus”, Or “hmmm, I’m swiping back and forth on my phone homescreens while I figure out what I want to do”,

This in-between time is a great time for fidgeting.

One way that Kinopio designs for fidget-ability is having cards ‘stick’ to your cursor when you hover over them. Once you get too far away, they bounce back.

There’s a handful of little details that make this fun without getting in your way.

  • sticking only starts after your mouse has rested on a card for ~200ms to prevent things feeling too sticky.
  • Cards stop sticking when you’re near a clickable button on a card, like a tag, a link, or a todo checkbox, so you can still be precise when it matters.

This also happens to be an example of a feature that couldn’t be conceived through mockups, and required a lot of fine-tuning with real code to make work well and feel good.

Principle #3

Embrace Plain Text

Text – even markdown – is not just for nerds and programmers. Text and full URLs are atomic units of computing: it’s copy-able, paste-able, and the most flexible way to share.

Embracing plain text also helps you turn regular people into power users because they can build on top of the skills (like ctrl-c, ctrl-v) they already have.

In Kinopio, almost everything in a card is just text that supports basic **markdown**, and a couple other custom syntaxes like [[ for tags, or a file or website URL.

When the card name changes, a hyper-fast custom parser (i.e. a crap ton of regexes) splits the text into html segments based on whether that text is plain text or a special content type like bolded text, tags, an image URL, or any other kind of URL. and uses those segments to render the front of the card.

This parser and segment system is some of the most complex code in the app – but I like that the effect feels effortless to everyone else.

Principle #4

A Single Interface for Mobile and Desktop

One of my pet peeves is the premise that if you’re viewing something on your phone that must mean you need a ‘clean’ minimal experience.

Platform Supported
Desktop Everything
Mobile ☹ Read only, or a quick entry UI only

Screw minimal – I want to do real work wherever I want. This is how it should be:

Platform Supported
Desktop Everything
Mobile Everything

Building an interface that works everywhere requires considerations that you need to bake in from day one this principle means that you can’t rely on hover to reveal controls. You need tappable alternatives to keyboard driven commands. And, of course, there’s way less room to fit things into – especially when the onscreen keyboard is up.

Related: The Hybrid Architecture of Kinopio for iOS

Principle #5

Refine by Pruning

Another habit I picked up at Glitch was to upload old mockups and screenshots somewhere that I can reference later.

When I go back in time to something like this original version of the card editing view, I’m reminded of the basicness of it.

Back then cards had fewer options: you could only remove the card, or add a decorative frame. Although I much prefer the flexibility of cards today, it’s undeniable that there was much less to figure out back then.

Inspired by this, I habitually re-evaluate whether features are still needed and used often enough to justify their existence.

Here are just two big features I’ve removed over the years:

Removed: Minimap [2 Weeks of Work]

Hold shift down or click the button in the bottom right to toggle on the minimap. Drag the window around to adjust your view, or tap anywhere to jump.

Unfortunately, no one really used the minimap because it was out of sight and mostly out of mind. I considered placing a persistent minimap in the corner but doing so compromised the feeling of a sense of place within a space (and it wouldn’t fit on a mobile screen anyways). After adding space zoom out I removed minimaps because they were now redundant.

Removed: Save Twitter/X Threads [3 Weeks of Work]

Import Twitter threads into your spaces from a tweet card. Or create new thread spaces by replying to on Twitter with @kinopioClub save

There are whole entire products built around saving Twitter/X threads, and people had requested it, so I was confident this would be a win.

But after all that work, tweets were being saved only once or twice a day. So after Twitter/X became increasingly hostile to developers, it was an easy choice to delete all Twitter/X-specific features from Kinopio.

Both of these features demo-ed really well and got a lot of likes on social media. But in the real world, all they did was take up valuable UI space, and their code would inevitably become a maintenance burden.

🔪 The most satisfying and direct way to handle complexity is to excise it like a tumor. But removing things has it’s own problems and needs it’s own special considerations and process…

The problem with removing things of course is that every feature has at least one person that relies on it. So it’s impossible to just remove something without someone feeling bad.

Compounding the problem, the longer things stay the same, the more people get attached to them working the same way. So the older and more advanced a tool gets, the harder change naturally becomes.

This makes pruning hard work – but it’s also an opportunity to build and strengthen the community around a tool.

  1. Share what you’re thinking of removing and why. The people most passionate about your product want to be as close to decisions as possible. I’d post this in Discord and on the Forum.

  2. Listen to what everyone has to say. See where the feature fits in their workflows and whether there’s an alternative way they could accomplish what they want to do.

  3. Be prepared to be wrong and change your mind if you overlooked something.

The hard part of being a designer or a coder isn’t design or code – it’s convincing people, and understanding and responding to their concerns and criticism.

Good principles exist to make you feel pain before your users do. They should guide and constrain you into thinking creatively about how to handle complexity.

Special thanks to Aneesha and Xhfloz for helping edit this.

item.title: Sam Altman – The Joe Rogan Experience
item.description:
Score 4 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @wseqyrku
October 8, 2023 | https://podcastdisclosed.com/2044-sam-altman-the-joe-rogan-experience/ | archive.org

🔑 Key Takeaways

  1. As AI advances, it has the power to improve lives, but it is important to consider the impact on individuals who may lose their jobs. Measures like UBI can provide temporary support, but addressing core needs and ensuring equitable access are crucial.
  2. The idea of an AI government raises important questions about our broken system and the need for change, but it is crucial to carefully consider safety measures and global regulations to prevent co-optation or compromise.
  3. Understanding and co-designing the societal impact of AGI and neural interfaces is crucial in order to create a fair and inclusive future, considering both the advantages and disadvantages that these technologies may bring.
  4. It is crucial to contemplate the implications of a technologically dominant reality, emphasizing the need for a balance between digital and human experiences, and ensuring privacy protection in the face of advancing technology.
  5. Balancing regulation and innovation is crucial in the development of financial systems, while the concept of cryptocurrencies challenges traditional notions of money and prompts reflection on information and wealth distribution.
  6. While advancements in technology and biological reengineering have the potential to eliminate negative emotions and promote innovation, it is important to foster a spirit of striving, risk-taking, and challenging the status quo for societal progress.
  7. Societal changes, such as the rise of technology and plastic use, have potential consequences including a feminization of males, decreased birth rates, and a shift towards a more peaceful yet potentially less fulfilling society.
  8. Our current societal values and biological instincts may change as technology progresses, questioning the need for physical dominance and violence. It is important to consider the possibility of overcoming our biological base for a more fulfilling and meaningful existence.
  9. By addressing societal issues like war and environmental factors, and embracing technological advancements like telepathic technology, we can engineer a more enlightened and resilient society.
  10. Social media platforms can contribute to mental health issues and online bullying, affecting both men and women. The addictive nature of scrolling and algorithmic feeds foster negativity instead of positive connections.
  11. Engaging in negative interactions and trolling on social media can be tempting and rewarding on a biological level, but it is unproductive and psychologically detrimental. The COVID-19 pandemic has worsened these negative tendencies, leading to increased anxiety and loss of sanity.
  12. Developing AGI is a milestone towards achieving our goals, but safety and alignment must be ensured. AGI can accelerate scientific knowledge for sustainable economic growth, but it is crucial to maintain control and collective will for the greater good.
  13. The conversation highlights the potential merging of humans with AI while discussing the need to disconnect from technology for mental well-being, emphasizing the unique challenges and opportunities of this era.
  14. Our constant attachment to phones can hinder our mental well-being and presence in the moment. Finding ways to regulate exposure to social media and disturbing content is essential for a healthier relationship with technology.
  15. The development of neural interfaces holds tremendous promise for neurological conditions, but it's vital to approach these advancements with an open mind, empathy, and a willingness to consider different perspectives.
  16. Psychedelic therapy shows promise in improving mental health and altering perceptions, but careful consideration of risks, appropriate screening, and guidance is crucial. The paradox between harmful and beneficial drug accessibility is evident.
  17. Addressing addiction requires a comprehensive approach, including legal changes, societal shifts towards understanding and support, counseling and therapy, and exploring alternative treatments.
  18. A careful approach, societal discussions, and responsible implementation are crucial to mitigate negative impacts and power imbalances caused by powerful substances and technologies.
  19. As technology advances, it is crucial to understand and navigate the potential consequences while ensuring that the benefits are accessible to all, leading to better choices and advancements in society.
  20. With increased access to information and advancements in technology, we have the potential to create an indistinguishable simulation and potentially become god-like beings in the future.
  21. As technology advances, it raises the question of whether our creations will eventually surpass us and become god-like forces. It also highlights the importance of learning from the past and avoiding repeating past mistakes.
  22. The cataclysmic event 11,800 years ago, supported by physical evidence and ancient texts, suggests the cyclical nature of civilization and the need for global cooperation in addressing AI safety concerns.
  23. Despite ongoing problems, violence has decreased over time, giving hope for the future. Embracing technological advancements can help us address and solve these problems more effectively for a better and safer world.

📝 Podcast Summary

The Potential of AI in Transforming Society and the Need for Equitable Distribution and Access

The advancement of science and technology, particularly in the field of artificial intelligence (AI), has the potential to bring about a world of abundance and improve people's lives. The cost of intelligence and the availability of abundant resources will play a crucial role in transforming society for the better. However, as AI replaces jobs in various sectors, there is a need to mitigate the negative impact on individuals who rely on those jobs. Implementing measures such as universal basic income (UBI) or other forms of long-term unemployment insurance can provide temporary economic support. Yet, addressing the core needs of individuals, such as agency, self-determination, and the ability to contribute meaningfully to society, is equally essential. It is crucial to not only distribute the benefits of AI but also ensure shared decision-making and access to these technological systems.

Exploring the Potential of an Unbiased AI Government

There is a growing interest in the possibility of an artificial intelligence (AI) government that is unbiased, rational, and equipped with the collective knowledge of humanity. This AI government could make objective decisions and optimize for the preferences of citizens, free from the influence of special interests and corruption. While this idea is still far from becoming a reality, it raises important questions about the current broken system and the need for change. However, it is essential to ensure that such a system does not become co-opted or compromised. The development of AI systems with AGI capabilities requires careful consideration of safety measures and global regulations. Despite the challenges, there is optimism about the progress being made in taking AI seriously, reminiscent of the discussions around nuclear weapons development. The rapid emergence of AI technology in public consciousness highlights the need for increased awareness and understanding of its potential implications.

Addressing challenges and questions in advancing technology

As technology continues to advance, there are important societal questions and challenges that need to be addressed. The development of AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) and neural interfaces raise concerns about fairness, individual choices, and the impact on those who choose not to adopt these technologies. It is crucial that we take the time to understand and co-design the society we want with these advancements, rather than rushing into their implementation. While the progression from each new technology iteration may seem incremental, the overall impact can be substantial. The development of external neural interfaces, even in their early stages, has the potential to enhance human capabilities and provide valuable tools. However, we must also consider the potential advantages and disadvantages that early adopters may have over the general population.

The Future of Human-Machine Fusion and the Balance of Digital and Human Experiences

Advancements in technology, particularly in the realm of neural interfaces and virtual reality, are leading us towards a future where we may choose to merge with machines and become cyborgs. While this may offer exciting possibilities, it also raises questions about the balance between the benefits of such advancements and the value of human experiences and the physical world. It is essential to consider the implications of a technologically dominated reality and ensure we maintain a balance between digital and human experiences. Additionally, technology plays a significant role in combating corruption, as it exposes hidden activities and makes it harder to conceal wrongdoing. However, we must also be cautious of the potential rise in surveillance and ensure the protection of privacy.

Central Bank Digital Currency, Regulation, and the Future of Money

Both Sam Altman and Joe Rogan express concerns about the potential negative impacts of central bank digital currency and the control it could have over society. They also discuss the importance of regulation in preventing situations like the FTX scandal. However, they both agree that there should be enough regulation to safeguard depositors' money without stifling innovation. The conversation then shifts to the concept of cryptocurrencies, particularly Bitcoin, as a potential global currency outside the control of any government. They discuss the possibility of a future where information is freely shared and accessible, leading to questions about the purpose and distribution of money. Overall, this conversation highlights the need for thoughtful consideration of financial systems and the potential implications of evolving technologies.

Exploring the potential of enhancing human biology for a more innovative and creative society

There is a fear that if people are given free money through initiatives like universal basic income, they will become lazy and lose their ambition. However, with advancements in technology and the ability to reengineer the human biological system, it may be possible to eliminate these concerns. By enhancing the human biological vehicle through coding and raising dopamine levels, it could be possible to eliminate negative emotions like anger, fear, and hate. Additionally, if everyone were to be on a low dose of Molly, it could promote a society where competition is replaced by a focus on innovation, creation, and creativity. However, it is important to remember that striving, risk-taking, and an explorer spirit are also crucial for society's progress. We need young visionaries who are not afraid to challenge the status quo and push forward with controversial ideas.

The impact of societal changes on males, birth rates, and human integration with technology.

Societal changes, such as the introduction of technology and the widespread use of plastic, may be causing a feminization of the males of the species and a decrease in birth rates. This can be seen as a potential facilitator for the integration of the human species with technology. While this may lead to a more peaceful and less aggressive society, it also raises concerns about the loss of certain important impulses, such as the drive to defend ourselves and our society. Additionally, this societal shift may contribute to a decrease in overall happiness. The lack of young founders in various fields, including technology startups, may be indicative of this long-term societal change.

The Evolution of Masculinity and the Potential Obsolescence of Violence

Our societal values surrounding masculinity and the need for physical strength may be rooted in our biological imperative to defend ourselves against threats. However, as technology advances and we potentially merge into a single consciousness, violence and physical dominance may become obsolete. While some may argue that these deep-seated aspects of human nature cannot be easily pushed aside, there is a possibility that our current biological system is not optimal and that we should be open to the idea of overcoming our biological base. Additionally, consumerism and the desire for newer and better things play a role in advancing technology and improving various aspects of our lives. Ultimately, there is a question of whether our current existence is fulfilling and meaningful, considering the rise in depression, anxiety, and existential angst.

Redefining Humanity: Engineering Enlightenment and Resilience

The biological reality of being a human doesn't align well with the world we've created. The solution might not lie in finding meaning within our biological vessel, but rather in engineering out the problematic aspects that hinder true enlightenment. The primary problem that plagues our species is war, the idea that it's acceptable to send groups of people to murder other groups due to government or superficial reasons. To address this, we could engineer out the human reward systems linked to acquiring resources. As we become a new thing, we might seek interaction with even more advanced beings. Scientific curiosity can fuel progress, but we must also acknowledge and address the environmental factors, like microplastics, contributing to the decline in testosterone and disrupting our endocrine system. Overall, we have the ability to make ourselves more resilient through choices and effort, but the widespread societal disruption of the endocrine system demands attention and action. Implementing telepathic technology could promote empathy and drastically reduce violence, both physical and emotional, that continues to plague our evolving society.

The negative impact of social media on mental health and well-being.

Social media and the constant scrolling through platforms like Instagram and Twitter can have detrimental effects on our mental health and overall well-being. The introduction of social media and smartphones has exacerbated problems such as self-harm, suicide, and online bullying. It's not just young girls who are affected, but also men. Famous people, who are often the target of negativity, have learned to become numb to it or disengage completely. Scrolling through endless feeds is often unfulfilling, yet we struggle to put down our phones. The algorithmic feeds intentionally feed us some interesting content amidst the mass of low-quality content. This new communication technology hijacks our human reward systems and fosters negativity and hate rather than the positive connections of traditional communication methods. Overall, we are still trying to navigate this technology without the tools or societal norms to modulate it effectively.

The Negative Impact of Social Media on Mental Health and Well-being

Social media platforms, like Twitter, can have a negative impact on people's mental health and overall well-being. Joe Rogan and Sam Altman discuss how engaging in negative interactions and trolling on these platforms can be tempting and even rewarding on a biological level. However, they both acknowledge that constantly engaging in such behavior is unproductive and psychologically detrimental. They highlight how the isolation caused by the COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated these negative tendencies, leading to further anxiety and loss of sanity for some individuals. While there are positive uses of social media, the majority of interactions tend to be negative. The conversation also touches upon the potential of future technology to revolutionize communication, but raises questions about the potential consequences and trade-offs that may come with it.

The Long-term Project of Creating Advanced Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and Its Impact on Society

Creating advanced artificial general intelligence (AGI) is a long-term project that requires careful consideration of its impact on society. As Sam Altman explains, the development of AGI is not the endpoint, but rather a milestone towards achieving our goals. Safety and alignment are major concerns, as the consequences of something going wrong could be disastrous. Nevertheless, progress has been made in understanding how to make AI safe, although there is still work to be done. The potential positive impact of AGI lies in its ability to significantly accelerate scientific knowledge, which is crucial for sustainable economic growth and progress. However, it is essential to ensure that humanity remains in control and that AGI acts in the collective will of humanity for the greater good, without corruption or bias. Despite the moral complexities, Altman considers working on AGI to be an incredibly exciting opportunity. Looking ahead, the possibilities of future steps beyond AGI are highly anticipated.

Navigating Technology's Impact on Humanity: A Conversation between Joe Rogan and Sam Altman

Humanity is at a unique point in its existence, facing both exciting advancements and pressing challenges. The conversation between Joe Rogan and Sam Altman highlights the rapid progress of technology and the potential merging of humans with AI. While Altman believes that humans in some form will continue to exist for a long time, potentially venturing into the universe alongside AI, Rogan holds a more pessimistic view, predicting that human biology will be gradually transformed, similar to the adoption of clothes and other innovations. The discussion also touches on the importance of disconnecting from technology for the sake of mental well-being. Regardless of the outcome, it is clear that the current era combines opportunity and complexity unlike any other in history.

The Negative Impact of Phone Attachment on Mental Well-Being and Being Present in the Moment.

Our constant attachment to our phones can have negative impacts on our mental well-being and ability to be present in the moment. Joe Rogan shares his experience of being without a phone for a few days while on vacation and how liberating it was to not constantly feel the need to check his phone. The conversation also delves into the addictive nature of social media, particularly Instagram, and how it can expose us to disturbing and unsettling content. This raises questions about the role of technology and how it affects our perception of society and human behavior. It prompts us to consider whether we need to find ways to edit or regulate our exposure to such content in order to maintain a healthier relationship with technology.

Exploring the Potential and Risks of Neural Interfaces

Neural interfaces have the potential to revolutionize the way we understand and treat neurological conditions. The restoration of sight and enhanced cognitive function are just some of the incredible benefits that could be achieved. However, it's important to acknowledge that the full extent and implications of neural interfaces are still unknown. Opening this Pandora's box could lead to irreversible changes, similar to the advent of computers. Nonetheless, it's crucial to approach these advancements with neutrality and objectivity, allowing for a deeper understanding of differing perspectives. This mindset can foster empathy and compassion, as Joe Rogan reflects on his personal growth throughout his podcast journey. Additionally, the obstacles to the legalization of psychedelic therapy highlight the influence of ignorance and biased decision-making in our society.

Embracing Psychedelic Therapy: Transformations, Advocacy, and Dilemmas

Psychedelic therapy, particularly with substances like LSD and psilocybin, has been transformative for many individuals, including Sam Altman and Joe Rogan. They have experienced significant improvements in mental health and a profound shift in their perceptions and behaviors. Both of them advocate for making these substances more accessible for therapeutic purposes. However, they also acknowledge the complexities of legalizing all drugs, as some individuals may not be psychologically prepared to handle their effects. It is important to consider the potential risks and benefits and ensure appropriate screening and guidance for individuals seeking psychedelic therapy. Additionally, the conversation highlights the paradox of a society that permits harmful drugs like OxyContin while restricting access to potentially beneficial substances.

Exploring the Complexities of Drug Addiction and Substance Abuse

The issue of drug addiction and substance abuse is complex and multifaceted. The conversation between Joe Rogan and Sam Altman highlights the dangers of drugs like oxycontin and fentanyl, as well as the rise of cartels and the illegal drug trade. While some argue for the legalization of drugs like heroin as a means to address these problems, others emphasize the need for serious mitigation efforts and support systems such as counseling and therapy. Additionally, alternative treatments like ibogaine and psilocybin show promising results in helping individuals overcome addiction. The legalization and regulation of marijuana in some states also offers insights into the potential positive effects of drug legalization on society. Ultimately, addressing addiction requires a comprehensive approach that combines not only legal changes, but also societal shifts towards understanding and support.

Caution and Respect: Addressing Concerns about Powerful Substances and Technologies

Both Joe Rogan and Sam Altman express concerns about the misuse and potential negative impacts of powerful substances and technologies. They highlight the importance of approaching things with caution and respect. Joe Rogan discusses his psychedelic experience, realizing that focusing too much on the world's problems leads to anger and frustration. Sam Altman raises concerns about the misuse of psychedelics and the potential inequality that could arise from advanced technologies, such as neural interfaces. They both emphasize the need for societal discussions and careful implementation to avoid disproportionate power dynamics and further polarization. It is essential to consider the effects and implications of substances and technologies in the pursuit of a better future.

The Power and Control Dilemma: Advancements in Technology and Neural Enhancements Raise Concerns

As technology advances, particularly with the potential creation of neural enhancements and advanced AI systems like Chat GPT, it raises concerns about power and control. The ability to access massive amounts of computing power and obtain accurate forecasts in areas like the stock market can already grant certain individuals a significant advantage. However, the integration of neural interfaces could create a completely different being, with unimaginable possibilities and power. The challenge lies in understanding and navigating the impact of such advancements, ensuring that the benefits are accessible to all and not just a select few. Ultimately, the increased access to information and knowledge can lead to better choices and advancements in society, but it's important to consider the potential consequences and limitations of these technologies.

Questioning Reality and the Potential for Advancement

As humans, we have the potential to make better choices with increased access to information. Joe Rogan and Sam Altman discuss the idea that our existence may be like a program and our consciousness connected to a simulated experience. They speculate on the possibility of creating an indistinguishable simulation that offers a fair, equitable, and peaceful life experience, devoid of crime and violence. They also explore the idea that as we advance technologically, we may create an artificial intelligent life form that surpasses us in capabilities and reaches god-like status. The constant drive for innovation and the creation of better things fuels our progress. Ultimately, this discussion leaves us questioning the nature of reality and the potential for us to become something akin to gods.

The Limits of Human Innovation and the Potential of Advanced Intelligent Life

Human beings have a constant desire to innovate and push the boundaries of creativity and technological power. The conversation highlights the idea that as we continue to advance and create more intelligent technologies, they may surpass our own capabilities and become god-like forces. It raises the question of whether the universe itself is the creative force behind all life and everything, rather than a separate entity creating it. Additionally, it emphasizes the limitations of our primal minds and the potential for future generations to engineer out detrimental traits. It leaves us pondering the unimaginable possibilities of what advanced intelligent life could achieve in the future, while also reminding us of the importance of learning from the past and avoiding repeating past mistakes.

Cataclysmic Event and Flood Myths: Evidence of a Major Disaster 11,800 Years Ago

There is evidence suggesting that a major cataclysmic event occurred approximately 11,800 years ago, causing the melting of the ice caps and flooding over North America. This event has been linked to flood myths found in ancient texts like the Epic of Gilgamesh and the Bible. Physical evidence, such as high levels of Iridium and micro diamonds, supports the theory that multiple comet impacts caused this catastrophe. It is also believed that human civilization has faced setbacks throughout history, returning to primal states. The discussion also highlights the importance of addressing the safety and ethical concerns surrounding artificial intelligence (AI). It is crucial for nations to come together and establish global rules and safety standards to prevent any harmful use of AGI technology. Ultimately, the hope is for humanity to overcome its baser instincts and work together for a better future.

The world managed to avoid using atomic weapons for warfare since 1945, which is truly remarkable. The destructive capabilities of these weapons and the fear of mutually assured destruction have prevented their use on a global scale. This realization gives us hope for the future, demonstrating that despite the presence of huge problems in the world, violence has actually decreased over time. However, it seems controversial to acknowledge this positive trend, as many people are deeply engrossed in the idea of ongoing problems and find their identity in solving them. Overcoming this mindset and embracing technological advancements, such as artificial general intelligence, may allow us to address these problems even more effectively. Ultimately, it is through continuous improvement and innovation that we can create a better and safer world.

item.title: Current State of Open Source AI Book
item.description:
Score 3 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @dpbrinkm
October 8, 2023 | https://book.premai.io/state-of-open-source-ai/index.html | archive.org

Clarity in the current fast-paced mess of Open Source innovation [1]

As a data scientist/developer with a 9 to 5 job, it’s difficult to keep track of all the innovations. There’s been enormous progress in the field in the last year.

The guide covers all the most important categories in the Open Source AI space, from model evaluations to deployment. It includes a Glossary for you to quickly check definitions of new frameworks & tools.

A quick TL;DR overview is included at the top of each section. We outline the pros/cons and general context/background for each topic. Then we dive a bit deeper. Examples include data models were trained on, and deployment implementations.

Who is This Guide For?#

Prerequisites to Reading

You should already know the basic principles of MLOps [2, 3, 4], i.e. you should know that the traditional steps are:

  1. Data engineering (preprocessing, curation, labelling, sanitisation)

  2. Model engineering (training, architecture design)

  3. Automated testing (CI)

  4. Deployment/Automated Inference (CD)

  5. Monitoring (logging, feedback, drift detection)

You haven’t followed the most recent developments in open source AI over the last year, and want to catch up quickly. We go beyond just mentioning the models, but also include things such as changing infrastructure, licence pitfalls, and novel applications.

Table of Contents#

We’ve divided the open-source tooling, models, & MLOps landscape into the following chapters:

Chapter

Description

Licences

Weights vs Data, Commercial use, Fair use, Pending lawsuits

Evaluation & Datasets

Leaderboards & Benchmarks for Text/Visual/Audio models

Models

LLaMA 1 vs 2, Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, Persimmon, …

Unaligned Models

FraudGPT, WormGPT, PoisonGPT, WizardLM, Falcon

Fine-tuning

LLMs, Visual, & Audio models

Model Formats

ONNX, GGML, TensorRT

MLOps Engines

vLLM, TGI, Triton, BentoML, …

Vector Databases

Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, Redis, Chroma, …

Software Development toolKits

LangChain, LLaMA Index, LiteLLM

Desktop Apps

LMStudio, GPT4All, Koboldcpp, …

Hardware

NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm, Apple Silicon, Intel, TPUs, …

Contributing#

This source of this guide is available on GitHub at premAI-io/state-of-open-source-ai.

Feedback

The current open-source ecosystem is moving at light-speed. Spot something outdated or missing? Want to start a discussion? We welcome any of the following:

  • let us know in the comments at the end of each chapter

  • create issues

  • open pull requests

Editing the Book#

  • Using GitHub Codespaces, you can edit code & preview the site in your browser without installing anything (you may have to whitelist github.dev, visualstudio.com, github.com, & trafficmanager.net if you use an adblocker).

  • Alternatively, to run locally, open this repository in a Dev Container (most likely using VSCode).

  • Or instead, manually set up your own Python environment:

    pip install -r requirements.txt                           # setup
PYTHONPATH=. jupyter-book build --builder dirhtml --all . # build
python -m http.server -d _build/dirhtml                   # serve

    alternative: live rebuilding & serving (experimental)

    pip install -r requirements.txt sphinx-autobuild # setup
jupyter-book config sphinx .                     # config
sphinx-autobuild -b dirhtml . _build/dirhtml     # build-serve

Formatting#

  • Quickstart

  • Full reference

  • Create a new chapter:

    • create some-file.md (containing # Some File heading and {{ comments }} footer)

    • add - file: some-file to _toc.yml

    • add [](some-file) | summary to ToC

  • Images: use {figure}/{figure-md} with captions

    • inline ref

    • numbered ref: Fig. 1

    • custom ref: Figure 1 with caption "This is a figure caption"

    • please use premAI-io/static.premai.io to host images & data

  • Tables: use {table} with captions

  • Glossary term: GPU

    • custom inline text: GPUs

  • Citations:

    • add BibTeX entries to references.bib, e.g.:

      • blogs, wikis: @online

      • docs: @manual

      • journal articles, news articles: @article

      • conference proceedings: @proceedings

      • books: @book

      • whitepapers: @techreport

      • chapters/parts of larger work: @incollection, @inbook

      • drafts: @unpublished

    • citing things defined in references.bib: [1, 5]

    • GitHub links:

      • repos: premAI-io/state-of-open-source-ai

      • issues: premAI-io/state-of-open-source-ai#12

      • code (folder/file): premAI-io/state-of-open-source-ai:index.md

      • readme sections: premAI-io/prem-app#demo

  • New Sphinx extensions: append to requirements.txt and _config.yml:sphinx.extra_extensions

  • linkcheck false-positives: append to _config.yml:sphinx.config.linkcheck*

Contributors#

Anyone who adds a few sentences to a chapter is automatically mentioned in the respective chapter as well as below.

  • Editor: Casper da Costa-Luis (casperdcl)

    With a strong academic background as well industry expertise to backup his enthusiasm for all things open source, Casper is happy to help with all queries related to this book.

  • Maintainer: PremAI-io

    Our vision is to engineer a world where individuals, developers, and businesses can embrace the power of AI without compromising their privacy. We believe in a future where users retain ownership of their data, AND the models trained on it.

  • Citing this book: [1]

Conclusion#

All models are wrong, but some are useful

—G.E.P. Box [6]

Open Source AI represents the future of privacy and ownership of data. On the other hand, in order to make this happen a lot of innovation should come into place. In the last year, already the open-source community demonstrated how motivated they are in order to deliver quality models to the hands of consumers creating already few big innovations in different AI fields. At the same time, this is just the beginning. Many improvements in multiple directions must be made in order to compare the results with centralised solutions.

At Prem we are on a journey to make this possible, with a focus on developer experience and deployment for any sort of developers, from Web Developers with zero knowledge about AI to affirmed Data Scientist who wants to quickly deploy and try these new models and technologies in their existing infra without compromising privacy.

Glossary#

Alignment#

Aligned AI models must implement safeguards to be helpful, honest, and harmless [7]. This often involves supervised fine-tuning followed by RLHF See Unaligned Models and Fine-tuning.

Auto-regressive language model#

Applies AR to LLMs. Essentially a feed-forward model which predicts the next word given a context (set of words) [8].

BEC#

Business Email Compromise.

Benchmark#

A curated dataset and corresponding tasks designed to evaluate models’ real-world performance metrics (so that models can be compared to each other).

Copyleft#

A type of open licence which insists that derivatives of the IP must have the same licence. Also called “protective” or “reciprocal” [9].

Embedding#

See vector embedding.

Evaluation#

Assessing a model’s abilities using quantitative and qualitative performance metrics (e.g. accuracy, effectiveness, etc.) on a given task. See Evaluation & Datasets.

Fair Dealing#

A doctrine in UK & commonwealth law permitting use of IP without prior permission under certain conditions (typically research, criticism, reporting, or satire) [10]. See also fair use.

Fair Use#

A doctrine in US law permitting use of IP without prior permission (regardless of licence/copyright status) depending on 1) purpose of use, 2) nature of the IP, 3) amount of use, and 4) effect on value [11]. See also fair dealing.

Foundation model#

A model trained from scratch – likely on lots of data – to be used for general tasks or later fine-tuned for specific tasks.

GPU#

Graphics Processing Unit: hardware originally designed to accelerate computer image processing, but now often repurposed for embarrassingly parallel computational tasks in machine learning.

Hallucination#

A model generating output that is inexplicable by its training data.

IP#

Intellectual Property: intangible creations by humans (e.g. code, text, art), typically legally protected from use without permission of the author(s).

Leaderboard#

Ranking of models based on their performance metrics on the same benchmark(s), allowing fair task-specific comparison. See Comparison of Leaderboards.

LLM#

A Large Language Model is neural network (often a transformer containing billions of parameters) designed to perform tasks in natural language via fine tuning or prompt engineering.

MLOps#

Machine Learning Operations: best practices to run AI using software products & cloud services

MoE#

Mixture-of-Experts is a technique which uses one or more specialist model(s) from a collection of models (“experts”) to solve general problems. Not that this is different from ensemble models (which combine results from all models).

Open#

Ambiguous term that could mean “open source” or “open licence”. See Meaning of “Open”.

Permissive#

A type of open licence which allows reselling and closed-source modifications, and can often be used in larger projects alongside other licences. Usually, the only condition of use is citing the author by name.

Perplexity#

Perplexity is a metric based on entropy, and is a rough measure of the difficulty/uncertainty in a prediction problem.

Public Domain#

“Open” IP owned by nobody (often due to the author disclaiming all rights) and thus can be used by anyone without restrictions. Technically a disclaimer/non-licence. See Open licence subcategories.

RAG#

Retrieval Augmented Generation.

RLHF#

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback is often the second step in alignment (after supervised fine-tuning), where a model is rewarded or penalised for it outputs based on human evaluation. See Fine-tuning and Unaligned Models.

ROME#

The Rank-One Model Editing algorithm alters a trained model’s weights to directly modify “learned” information [12, 13].

SIMD#

Single Instruction, Multiple Data is a data-level parallel processing technique where one computational instruction is applied to multiple data simultaneously.

SotA#

State of the art: recent developments (under 1 year old).

Supervised fine-tuning#

SFT is often the first step in model alignment, and is usually followed by RLHF. See Fine-tuning and Unaligned Models.

Quantisation#

Sacrificing precision of model weights (e.g. uint8 instead of float32) in return for lower hardware memory requirements.

Token#

A token is a “unit of text” for an LLM to process/generate. A single token could represent a few characters or words, depending on the tokenisation method chosen. Tokens are usually embedded.

Transformer#

A transformer is a neural network using a parallel multi-head attention mechanism. The resultant reduce training time makes it well-suited for use in LLMs.

Vector Database#

Vector databases provide efficient storage & search/retrieval for vector embeddings. See Vector Databases.

Vector Embedding#

Embedding means encoding tokens into a numeric vector (i.e. array/list). This can be thought of as an intermediary between machine and human language, and thus helps LLMs understand human language. See LLM Embeddings.

Vector Store#

See vector database.

item.title: Simplifying Development Environments with Nix
item.description:
Score 4 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @shahinism
October 8, 2023 | https://shahin.blog/introducing-devenv-templates-simplifying-development-environments-with-nix | archive.org

Over the past year, I've dived deep into the world of NixOS, discovering its robustness, flexibility, and power. I've crafted various configurations and setups tailored to my development needs during this journey. Today, I'm excited to introduce the devenv templates, a culmination of my learnings and experiences with NixOS.

Why devenv Templates?
The primary drive behind publishing these templates is twofold:

  1. Personal Convenience: I can rapidly bootstrap new projects without reinventing the wheel by standardizing my frequently-used configurations into templates.

  2. Community Benefit: I believe in the power of shared knowledge. By making these templates public, I hope to attract fellow developers, offering them a starting point and perhaps even igniting their interest in the Nix ecosystem.

No Barriers to Adoption
It's important to note that adopting these devenv templates is a non-invasive process. Team members who prefer not to use devenv it won't find their workflow disrupted. However, embracing devenv can significantly expedite migration processes and ensure consistent developer environments.

How Does It Compare?
When compared with other development environment solutions, devenv it showcases its true prowess. Apart from managing dependency packages, devenv it stands out by:

  • Composing Services: Need a database for your project? devenv You can set it up without dragging you into the intricate world of containerization – a particularly beneficial feature for Mac users who often grapple with container complexities.

  • Container Compatibility: While devenv It eases the process by avoiding unnecessary containerization; it's not opposed to it. You can effortlessly export your environment into containers when needed, providing flexibility for varied deployment scenarios.

The Power of Nix for Project Management

While the devenv templates offer an immediate window into a more streamlined development experience; it's crucial to understand the backbone that powers this simplicity: Nix. Leveraging Nix for project management ushers in an array of benefits:

  1. Reproducibility: At its core, Nix prioritizes reproducibility. It ensures that your projects are built the same way every single time, irrespective of where they're run. This uniformity eliminates the dreaded "it works on my machine" problem.

  2. Isolation: Each project managed by Nix operates in its isolated environment. This compartmentalization ensures that dependencies, libraries, or tools used in one project don't interfere with another.

  3. Atomic Upgrades and Rollbacks: Nix's approach to managing updates is atomic. This means any upgrade or change either fully succeeds or fails without side effects, thus ensuring that there's never a halfway or broken state. If an update isn't to your liking, rolling back to a previous state is just as straightforward.

  4. Declarative Configuration: With Nix, your project's setup is defined clearly. This clarity not only aids readability but also simplifies the onboarding process for new team members. They can set up their development environment to mirror the project's requirements with minimal friction.

  5. Efficient Dependency Management: Nix innovatively handles dependencies, storing them in the Nix store. This approach ensures multiple projects can share common dependencies without redundancy while maintaining their isolated environments.

  6. Cross-Platform Compatibility: While devenv templates are a boon; Nix's compatibility across different Unix systems further ensures that your project's setup remains consistent, be it on macOS, Linux, or any other Unix-like system.

Incorporating Nix into your project management workflow thus translates to consistency, reliability, and efficiency. It's not merely a tool but a paradigm shift in perceiving and handling project dependencies and environments.

Conclusion

In conclusion, the devenv templates are not just a product of my journey with NixOS but a testament to the potential of the Nix ecosystem. Whether you're a seasoned Nix user or a curious developer, I invite you to explore these templates and experience a streamlined development setup.

item.title: Evaluating 55 LLMs with GPT-4
item.description:
Score 36 | Comments 8 (thread link) | @vincelt
October 8, 2023 | https://benchmarks.llmonitor.com/leaderboard | archive.org

leaderboard | dataset | compare | about


Traditional LLMs benchmarks have drawbacks: they quickly become part of training datasets and are hard to relate to in terms of real-world use-cases.

I made this as an experiment to address these issues. Here, the dataset is dynamic (changes every week) and composed of crowdsourced real-world prompts.

We then use GPT-4 to grade each model's response against a set of rubrics (more details on the about page). The prompt dataset is easily explorable.

Everything is then stored in a Postgres database and this page shows the raw results.
